title: Closure of the Global Overturning Circulation Through the Indian, Pacific, and Southern Oceans: Schematics and Transports
problem: Existing conceptual models of the global overturning circulation are often incomplete, as they overemphasize wind-driven upwelling in the Southern Ocean while neglecting the essential role of deep, diapycnal mixing in the Indian and Pacific Oceans required to close the global heat and volume budget.
method: This paper proposes a quantitative, heat- and mass-balanced schematic for the global overturning circulation by analyzing meridional transports from hydrographic data to synthesize the roles of Southern Ocean wind-driven upwelling and deep diapycnal transformation in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
task: The task is to describe the pathways and energetics of the global overturning circulation, presenting updated schematics and quantitative transports to explain its closure through the Indian, Pacific, and Southern Oceans.
innovation: This paper provides updated schematics and transport quantifications for the global overturning circulation, demonstrating the essential role of deep diapycnal mixing in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, in addition to Southern Ocean upwelling, for closing the global heat and volume budgets.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: ABSTRACT. The overturning pathways for the surface-ventilated North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) and Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) and the diffusively formed Indian Deep Water (IDW) and Pacific Deep Water (PDW) are intertwined. The global overturning circulation (GOC) includes both large wind-driven upwelling in the Southern Ocean and important internal diapycnal transformation in the deep Indian and Pacific Oceans. All three northern-source Deep Waters (NADW, IDW, PDW) move southward and upwell in the Southern Ocean. AABW is produced from the denser, salty NADW and a portion of the lighter, low oxygen IDW/PDW that upwells above and north of NADW. The remaining upwelled IDW/PDW stays near the surface, moving into the subtropical thermoclines, and ultimately sources about one-third of the NADW. Another third of the NADW comes from AABW upwelling in the Atlantic. The remaining third comes from AABW upwelling to the thermocline in the Indian-Pacific. Atlantic cooling associated with NADW formation (0.3 PW north of 32°S; 1 PW = 1015 W) and Southern Ocean cooling associated with AABW formation (0.4 PW south of 32°S) are balanced mostly by 0.6 PW of deep diffusive heating in the Indian and Pacific Oceans; only 0.1 PW is gained at the surface in the Southern Ocean. Thus, while an adiabatic model of NADW global overturning driven by winds in the Southern Ocean, with buoyancy added only at the surface in the Southern Ocean, is a useful dynamical idealization, the associated heat changes require full participation of the diffusive Indian and Pacific Oceans, with a basin-averaged diffusivity on the order of the Munk value of 10-4 m² s¯¹.

INTRODUCTION
Description of the pathways and energet-ics of the global overturning circulation (GOC) is central to understanding the interaction of different ocean basins and layers as well as the interplay of external forcings. Changes in the ocean's overturn on decadal to millennial time scales are central to variations in Earth's climate. For many decades, the dominant para-digm of the global overturning circula-tion described two nearly independent cells: the popularized North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) “great ocean con-veyor,” with the formation of NADW in the northern North Atlantic returned by upwelling in the Indian and Pacific Oceans (Gordon, 1986a; Broecker, 1987), and a second cell associated with Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) for-mation in the south (Gordon, 1986b, 1991; Broecker, 1991; Schmitz, 1995). Connection of the two through upwell-ing of AABW into NADW in the North Atlantic has long been an accepted part of the global volume transport budget.

This 0.83 PW of warming in the Indian and Pacific is offset by -0.70 PW of cooling of upper thermocline waters exiting the Agulhas, south of 32°S, before they enter the South Atlantic, adding to 0.13 PW, which is within round-off error of the required 0.14 PW. It was long ago noted (Rintoul, 1991) that northward upper ocean flow in the South Atlantic is significantly cooler than the warm Agulhas southward flow. The large cool-ing of the surface waters occurs along the north side of the Agulhas Return Current (Large and Yeager, 2009; Cerovečki et al., 2011) and advects much of the Agulhas water southeastward toward Kerguelen. This cooled water joins the eastward flow of SAMW north of the ACC. The final product, SAMW/ AAIW, flows northward in the South Atlantic, dominating the return to the Atlantic of upper ocean waters that feed into the NADW cell.
